items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A 68-year-old man reports bone pain, a hat that no longer fits, and hearing loss. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly raised, while calcium, phosphate, and PTH are normal. Which histologic finding is expected in affected bone?
options: Fibrous tissue with hemosiderin-laden giant cells
Mosaic pattern of woven and lamellar bone
items.rationale: Paget disease of bone (osteitis deformans) is localized remodeling with excess osteoclastic and then osteoblastic activity that forms poor-quality bone; calcium, phosphorus, and PTH are normal, ALP is raised, the bone shows a mosaic of woven and lamellar bone, and skull thickening enlarges hat size and causes hearing loss.
expl: Unmineralized osteoid seams indicate osteomalacia.
Fibrous tissue with hemosiderin-laden giant cells forms the brown tumors of hyperparathyroidism.
Thin trabeculae with normal mineralization describe osteoporosis.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A 12-year-old boy has a painful diaphyseal femoral mass with an onion-skin periosteal reaction. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells. Which finding confirms the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Ewing sarcoma, usually in boys under 15, arises in the diaphysis of long bones or the pelvis, shows anaplastic small blue cells, and produces an onion-skin periosteal reaction; testing for t(11;22) and its EWS-FLI1 fusion separates it from lymphoma and chronic osteomyelitis.
expl: t(2;13) with PAX3-FOXO1 fusion defines alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
t(X;18) with SS18-SSX fusion defines synovial sarcoma.
MYCN (N-myc) amplification marks aggressive neuroblastoma.

items.rationale: Dermatomyositis, with proximal muscle weakness, Gottron papules, and a heliotrope rash, is a paraneoplastic association of adenocarcinomas, especially ovarian, so an occult malignancy should be sought.
expl: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A 62-year-old smoker has proximal leg weakness that improves briefly with repeated effort, dry mouth, constipation, and depressed reflexes. A central lung mass is found. Against which target are the autoantibodies directed?
items.rationale: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is caused by autoantibodies to presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels that reduce acetylcholine release; it causes proximal weakness that improves with use, autonomic symptoms, and hyporeflexia, and it is associated with small cell lung cancer.
expl: Anti-Hu antibodies cause paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis with small cell lung cancer.
Antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, whose weakness worsens with use.
Antibodies to muscle-specific tyrosine kinase cause a subset of receptor-antibody-negative myasthenia gravis.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A 25-year-old man has chronic low back pain and morning stiffness that improve with exercise. Radiographs show bilateral sacroiliitis and vertebral fusion, and he has had anterior uveitis. Which cardiac lesion is associated with his disease?
items.rationale: Ankylosing spondylitis is an HLA-B27-associated spondyloarthropathy with symmetric spine and sacroiliac involvement leading to fusion (bamboo spine), uveitis, and aortitis that causes aortic regurgitation.
expl: Mitral stenosis is a late sequel of rheumatic heart disease.
Tricuspid regurgitation follows right ventricular dilation, endocarditis in injection drug use, or carcinoid heart disease.
Pulmonic stenosis is usually congenital or part of carcinoid heart disease.

items.stem: An older adult has several well-demarcated, verrucous, brown plaques on the trunk that look stuck on. Histology shows immature keratinocytes with keratin-filled horn cysts. What is the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Seborrheic keratosis is a well-demarcated, verrucous, benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes with keratin-filled horn cysts that looks stuck on; a sudden eruption of many lesions (Leser-Trélat sign) may signal an internal malignancy such as GI adenocarcinoma.
expl: Actinic keratosis is a rough, sun-induced premalignant papule with keratinocyte dysplasia.
A melanocytic nevus is a benign proliferation of melanocytes without horn cysts.
Superficial spreading melanoma shows atypical melanocytes spreading through the epidermis.

items.rationale: Acanthosis nigricans is epidermal hyperplasia producing symmetric, hyperpigmented, velvety thickening of the axilla or neck; it is associated with insulin resistance (diabetes, obesity, Cushing syndrome, PCOS) and with visceral malignancy such as gastric adenocarcinoma.
expl: Celiac disease is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis.
Adrenal insufficiency causes diffuse hyperpigmentation of skin and mucosa.
Hepatitis C infection is associated with lichen planus and porphyria cutanea tarda.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a drug-induced necrotizing eruption with mucosal involvement and a positive Nikolsky sign.

items.stem: Compared with skin affected by vitiligo, skin from a patient with oculocutaneous albinism shows which feature?
options: Normal melanocyte number with reduced melanin
Melanocytes that failed to arise from neural crest
items.rationale: Albinism has a normal number of melanocytes with reduced melanin production from decreased tyrosinase activity or defective tyrosine transport; vitiligo is destruction of melanocytes, believed to be autoimmune, producing irregular patches of complete depigmentation.

items.stem: Two decades after a deep burn, a chronic nonhealing ulcer in the scar becomes indurated with rolled edges. Biopsy shows invasive atypical keratinocytes forming keratin pearls. What is this lesion called?
items.rationale: A Marjolin ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or scar, usually more than 20 years after the injury; squamous cell carcinoma is also associated with immunosuppression and arsenic exposure and shows keratin pearls.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A young adult develops targetlike skin lesions with dusky centers on the palms and extremities a week after a recurrent cold sore. Mucosal involvement is minimal, and there is no fever. What is the diagnosis?
items.rationale: Erythema multiforme is associated with infections such as HSV and Mycoplasma pneumoniae and with drugs; it presents with macules, papules, vesicles, and target lesions with dusky centers, while Stevens-Johnson syndrome adds fever, mucosal involvement, and skin necrosis with sloughing, usually from a drug.
expl: Urticaria produces transient pruritic wheals from mast cell degranulation.
Pityriasis rosea begins with a herald patch followed by scaly plaques in a Christmas-tree distribution.
Stevens-Johnson syndrome causes fever, mucosal involvement, bullae, and sloughing, usually after a drug.

items.rationale: Schwannoma arises from Schwann cells, classically at the cerebellopontine angle on CN VIII (vestibular schwannoma) with hearing loss and tinnitus; it is S-100-positive with biphasic hypercellular (Antoni A) and hypocellular myxoid (Antoni B) areas, and bilateral tumors occur in NF2.
expl: Ependymoma most often arises in the fourth ventricle with perivascular pseudorosettes.
Neurofibroma is an unencapsulated nerve sheath tumor typical of NF1.
Meningioma is a dural-based arachnoid cell tumor with whorls and psammoma bodies.

items.stem: A 9-year-old has headache and ataxia from a well-circumscribed cerebellar tumor that is cystic with a mural nodule. Histology shows bipolar cells with hairlike processes and eosinophilic corkscrew fibers. What is the tumor?
items.rationale: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common primary brain tumor of childhood, usually a well-circumscribed posterior fossa tumor that is cystic with a mural nodule; it is GFAP-positive, with bipolar hairlike cells, microcysts, and Rosenthal fibers, and it has a good prognosis.
expl: Hemangioblastoma shows closely packed thin-walled capillaries and is linked to von Hippel-Lindau syndrome.
Ependymoma shows perivascular pseudorosettes and blepharoplasts.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A young adult has a cerebellar tumor of closely packed thin-walled capillaries, bilateral retinal angiomas, and a raised hematocrit. Which gene is mutated?
items.rationale: Hemangioblastoma, most often cerebellar, consists of closely arranged thin-walled capillaries; with retinal angiomas it indicates von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (VHL deletion on chromosome 3p), and tumor erythropoietin can cause secondary polycythemia.
expl: NF1 on chromosome 17 causes neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, and optic gliomas.
NF2 on chromosome 22 causes bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas.
TSC2 on chromosome 16 causes tuberous sclerosis with cortical tubers and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A 10-year-old has headaches, growth failure, and bitemporal hemianopia. Imaging shows a calcified cystic mass above the sella containing fluid like machinery oil with cholesterol crystals. From which structure does the tumor arise?
items.rationale: Craniopharyngioma, the most common supratentorial tumor of childhood, derives from remnants of Rathke pouch (ectoderm); it is often calcified, contains cholesterol crystals in motor-oil-like fluid, compresses the chiasm to cause bitemporal hemianopia, and recurs often.
expl: Arachnoid cap cells give rise to meningioma.
Pineal germ cell tumors compress the cerebral aqueduct and cause Parinaud syndrome.
Lactotroph adenomas are prolactinomas, which present with galactorrhea and amenorrhea and lack cholesterol-rich cyst fluid.

items.subject: Pathology
items.stem: A patient with chronic alcohol use and a serum sodium of 110 mEq/L receives hypertonic saline, and the sodium rises rapidly. Two days later the patient develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and quadriparesis that progress to a locked-in state. Where is the main lesion?
items.rationale: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) is massive demyelination of pontine white matter after rapid osmotic shifts, most often overly fast correction of hyponatremia; it causes acute paralysis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and diplopia and can produce a locked-in state.
expl: Medial medullary infarction causes contralateral hemiparesis with ipsilateral tongue deviation.
Internal capsule hemorrhage is a hypertensive stroke causing contralateral hemiparesis.
Mammillary body necrosis is the lesion of Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency.

items.stem: A drug's clearance falls by 50% while its volume of distribution doubles. How does its elimination half-life change?
items.rationale: Half-life equals 0.7 × Vd / CL; doubling Vd and halving CL each double the half-life, so it increases fourfold.
expl: A 75% fall would need clearance to rise or Vd to fall.
A twofold rise would follow from only one of the two changes.
Both changes lengthen the half-life.

expl: 6.25 pmol/L is the level after four half-lives.

options: Rate of elimination equals rate of administration

Drug elimination stops until the next dose

options: B is more potent; A is more efficacious
A is more potent and more efficacious
B is more potent and more efficacious
A is more potent; B is more efficacious
items.rationale: Potency reflects the dose for a given effect (lower EC50 means higher potency), and efficacy reflects the maximal effect; the two are unrelated, so Drug A is more potent and Drug B more efficacious.
expl: This reverses both properties.

Drug B needs a higher dose, so it is less potent.

An antagonist does not raise potency or efficacy.

expl: 0.025 inverts the ratio.

Drug Y's index of 10 is lower.

Switch to giving the dose by IV push
Slow the infusion and give diphenhydramine

A faster rate worsens the reaction.

Myasthenia gravis patients are relatively resistant to succinylcholine.
Hypercalcemia does not prolong paralysis.

Branching enzyme deficiency (Andersen) causes infantile cirrhosis with abnormal long-chain glycogen.

Fructose-1-phosphate traps phosphate, blocking glucose output
Lactate competes with glucose for hepatic uptake
Fructose suppresses glucagon release from alpha cells

The mechanism is phosphate trapping, not glucagon suppression.

options: A ketogenic diet high in fat, lysine, and leucine
A high-carbohydrate diet with frequent feeds

expl: Carbohydrate increases pyruvate load and worsens lactic acidosis.
Protein restriction with arginine treats urea cycle disorders.
Fructose restriction treats hereditary fructose intolerance.

Ketone bodies and urea are not products of pyruvate.

items.stem: A 3-day-old boy becomes lethargic and vomits. Plasma ammonia is very high, BUN is low, and urinary orotic acid is increased. The blood count is normal. Which enzyme is deficient?
items.rationale: Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common urea cycle disorder, causes hyperammonemia with low BUN; excess carbamoyl phosphate is diverted to orotic acid, and there is no megaloblastic anemia.

N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency inactivates CPS I, so orotic acid does not rise.
CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonemia without increased orotic acid, because carbamoyl phosphate is not formed.

expl: Glutamine rises in any hyperammonemia as ammonia is fixed.

items.stem: Excess ammonia in the brain inhibits the TCA cycle mainly by which mechanism?
items.rationale: Ammonia combines with alpha-ketoglutarate to form glutamate and then glutamine, lowering alpha-ketoglutarate and inhibiting the TCA cycle; glutamine also causes osmotic cerebral edema.
expl: Pyruvate carboxylase is not the site of ammonia toxicity.
Uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol dissipate the proton gradient; ammonia does not.
Cytochrome c oxidase is inhibited by cyanide and carbon monoxide, not ammonia.

It activates hepatic urea cycle enzymes
It acidifies the colon and traps ammonium

Lactulose does not act on hepatic enzymes.

items.stem: A child with a urea cycle defect receives sodium phenylbutyrate. How does this drug lower ammonia?
options: It supplies ornithine to restart the urea cycle
It binds glutamine into a renally excreted product
It acidifies the colon and traps ammonium
items.rationale: Phenylbutyrate (like benzoate and phenylacetate) reacts with glutamine or glycine to form products excreted by the kidney, removing nitrogen without the urea cycle.
expl: Phenylbutyrate does not supply urea cycle intermediates.
Colonic acidification is the action of lactulose.
Suppressing ammoniagenic bacteria is the action of rifaximin.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: Why does tyrosine become an essential amino acid in phenylketonuria?
options: Phenylalanine is not converted to tyrosine
Tyrosine is consumed by excess melanin synthesis
Tyrosine is lost in the urine as phenyl ketones
Tyrosine absorption is blocked by phenylalanine
items.rationale: Phenylalanine hydroxylase normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; when it is deficient, tyrosine must come from the diet.
expl: Melanin synthesis is reduced in PKU, which is why skin is hypopigmented.
Phenyl ketones are phenylalanine metabolites, not tyrosine losses.
The problem is lack of synthesis, not blocked absorption.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with phenylketonuria stopped her low-phenylalanine diet in adolescence and is now 6 weeks pregnant. Without dietary control, her fetus is at risk of which outcome?
options: Limb reduction defects of the arms
Open neural tube defects of the spine
items.rationale: High maternal phenylalanine in untreated PKU causes phenylalanine embryopathy: fetal growth restriction, microcephaly, intellectual disability, and congenital heart defects, preventable by dietary control.
expl: Limb reduction defects are linked to thalidomide.
Macrosomia with neonatal hypoglycemia follows maternal diabetes.
Neural tube defects are linked to folate deficiency and valproate.

items.rationale: Alkaptonuria, autosomal recessive deficiency of homogentisate oxidase, lets homogentisic acid build up: ochronosis of connective tissue, ear cartilage, and sclerae; urine darkening on exposure to air; and arthralgias.
expl: Cystathionine synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria.
Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency impairs catecholamine synthesis.
Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency causes PKU with hypopigmentation.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: A 12-year-old tall, thin boy with mild intellectual disability has downward and inward lens dislocation, osteoporosis, and a past deep vein thrombosis. Which defect is most likely?
items.rationale: Homocystinuria, most often from cystathionine synthase deficiency, causes marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis, downward and inward lens subluxation, thrombosis, and intellectual disability.
expl: Fibrillin-1 mutation (Marfan syndrome) causes upward and outward lens subluxation without thrombosis or intellectual disability.
Homogentisate oxidase deficiency causes ochronosis and arthralgias.
Type I collagen mutation (osteogenesis imperfecta) causes fractures and blue sclerae.

items.stem: Homocystinuria due to methionine synthase deficiency is treated with which dietary change?
items.rationale: Methionine synthase deficiency blocks remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, so dietary methionine is increased; decreased methionine is used for cystathionine synthase deficiency.
expl: Decreased methionine treats cystathionine synthase deficiency.
Cysteine is increased, not decreased, in cystathionine synthase deficiency.
Phenylalanine is unrelated to homocysteine metabolism.

Less methionine, more cysteine, B6, B12, and folate

expl: This reverses the methionine and cysteine changes.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: A 22-year-old has recurrent kidney stones. Urine microscopy shows hexagonal crystals, and the cyanide-nitroprusside test is positive. Reabsorption of which group of amino acids is defective?
items.rationale: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of the renal PCT and intestinal transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA); cystine precipitates as hexagonal stones and is detected by the cyanide-nitroprusside test.
expl: Aromatic amino acids are not the cystinuria transporter's substrates.
Glycine, proline, and hydroxyproline are lost in iminoglycinuria.
Branched-chain amino acids accumulate in maple syrup urine disease.

items.stem: Which measure increases the solubility of cystine in a patient with cystinuria?
items.rationale: Urinary alkalinization (potassium citrate, acetazolamide) and chelating agents such as penicillamine increase cystine solubility; hydration and a low-methionine diet also help.
expl: Allopurinol lowers uric acid, not cystine.
Methionine is a cystine precursor, so the diet is low in methionine.
Acidification lowers cystine solubility.

items.stem: A 5-day-old has poor feeding, vomiting, hypotonia, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypoglycemia, and hyperammonemia. Urine organic acids show 3-hydroxypropionate and methylcitrate, and methylmalonic acid is low. Which enzyme is deficient?
items.rationale: Propionic acidemia, from propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, raises propionyl-CoA and lowers methylmalonic acid; organic acid accumulation inhibits gluconeogenesis and the urea cycle, causing hypoglycemia, ketoacidosis, and hyperammonemia.
expl: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase deficiency raises methylmalonic acid.
OTC deficiency causes hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria, not an organic acidosis.
Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency causes lactic acidosis without propionate metabolites.

items.stem: A 6-month-old of Ashkenazi Jewish descent has developmental regression, an exaggerated startle to noise, and a cherry-red spot on the macula; the liver and spleen are not enlarged. Which substance accumulates in neurons?
items.rationale: Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) causes neurodegeneration, hyperacusis, and a cherry-red macular spot with GM2 ganglioside accumulation and no hepatosplenomegaly, unlike Niemann-Pick disease.
expl: Sphingomyelin accumulates in Niemann-Pick disease, which has hepatosplenomegaly.
Galactocerebroside accumulates in Krabbe disease, which has no cherry-red spot.
Glucocerebroside accumulates in Gaucher disease, which causes organomegaly and bone disease.

Protoporphyrin accumulates in lead poisoning.

expl: 1 in 100 is q, the allele frequency.

1 in 200 is half the carrier frequency.

options: Every daughter and no son affected
Every son and no daughter affected
Half of daughters and half of sons
items.rationale: In X-linked dominant inheritance, 100% of daughters and 0% of sons of affected fathers are affected, because fathers pass their X to every daughter and their Y to every son.

Half of each sex fits an affected heterozygous mother.

items.stem: Most cases of Down syndrome result from which mechanism?
items.rationale: About 95% of Down syndrome cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction, most commonly in meiosis I, increasing with maternal age.
expl: Postfertilization mitotic error causes about 1% of cases.
Uniparental disomy does not cause trisomy.
Robertsonian translocation causes about 4% of cases.

items.rationale: In incomplete penetrance, not all individuals with a pathogenic variant show the disease; BRCA1 mutations do not always cause breast or ovarian cancer.
expl: Locus heterogeneity means mutations at different genes cause one disease.
Anticipation means earlier onset in later generations.
Variable expressivity means affected people differ in severity.

items.stem: Two siblings with neurofibromatosis type 1 share the same mutation; one has a few café-au-lait spots, and the other has many neurofibromas and an optic glioma. Which genetic term applies?
items.rationale: In variable expressivity, patients with the same genotype have varying phenotypes, as in two patients with NF1 of differing severity.
expl: Incomplete penetrance would leave a carrier with no disease.
Pleiotropy is one gene affecting several traits in one person.
Anticipation is earlier onset in later generations, not siblings.

items.stem: A child inherits one mutant RB1 allele and develops retinoblastoma after the second allele is lost in a retinal cell. Which concept does this illustrate?
items.rationale: With a mutated tumor suppressor, the wild-type allele must be deleted or mutated before cancer develops (loss of heterozygosity, the two-hit hypothesis).
expl: Imprinting is parent-of-origin silencing.
Gain of function describes oncogenes.
A dominant negative protein blocks the normal protein from one allele.

items.stem: One mutant p53 allele makes a protein that binds DNA and blocks the normal p53 protein from binding its promoters. Which term describes this mutation?
items.rationale: A dominant negative mutation produces a nonfunctional protein that also prevents the normal gene product from working, as with a single mutated p53.
expl: Haploinsufficiency is disease from one missing functional copy without interference.
Gain of function adds a new or increased activity.
Loss of heterozygosity removes the remaining normal allele.

items.stem: Two children of healthy, unrelated parents have the same autosomal dominant disorder. Neither parent shows the trait, and DNA from parental blood is normal. What is the most likely explanation?
items.rationale: If parents and relatives do not have the disease, gonadal (germline) mosaicism should be suspected: the mutation is present only in egg or sperm cells.
expl: The disorder is autosomal dominant.
A nonpenetrant carrier parent would show the variant in blood DNA.
Uniparental disomy in two children is very unlikely and does not explain a dominant disorder.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: A 6-year-old girl has precocious puberty, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, and unilateral café-au-lait spots with ragged edges. Which mechanism explains her disease?
items.rationale: McCune-Albright syndrome is due to an activating Gs-protein (GNAS) mutation; it is lethal if present before fertilization but survivable with mosaicism.
expl: Maternal uniparental disomy 15 causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
RET mutations cause MEN2.
NF1 causes bilateral smooth-edged café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas.

items.stem: A child has an autosomal recessive disorder, but only the mother is a carrier, and paternity is confirmed. Which mechanism is most likely?
items.rationale: Isodisomy gives two identical copies of one parent's chromosome; it should be considered when a recessive disorder appears and only one parent is a carrier.
expl: Anticipation applies to repeat expansion disorders.
Paternal disomy would not carry the mother's mutation.
Incomplete penetrance does not create a second mutant allele.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: A small group settles an isolated island, and centuries later a rare recessive disease is common there. Which concept explains this?
items.rationale: The founder effect is a type of bottleneck from population separation; allele frequencies shift by chance (genetic drift), not by selection.
expl: Linkage disequilibrium concerns alleles inherited together.
Natural selection favors alleles that increase fitness.
Heterozygote advantage maintains alleles that protect carriers.

items.rationale: During development, one X chromosome in each XX cell is randomly inactivated and condensed into a Barr body (methylated heterochromatin).
expl: The nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.

items.stem: The CFTR gene mutated in cystic fibrosis is on which chromosome?
items.rationale: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, caused by a defect in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, most often the deltaF508 deletion.
expl: Chromosome 21 is trisomic in Down syndrome.
Chromosome 15 carries FBN1 and the Prader-Willi and Angelman region.
Chromosome 17 carries NF1, BRCA1, and TP53.

items.subject: Biochemistry
items.stem: The most common CFTR mutation, deletion of phenylalanine 508, causes disease mainly through which mechanism?
options: Normal protein with a closed gate
Misfolded protein fails to reach the membrane
Premature stop codon with no mRNA
Excess channel activity in sweat ducts
items.rationale: Phe508 deletion produces a misfolded protein with improper trafficking, so CFTR is absent from the cell membrane and chloride and water secretion fall.
expl: A gating defect is the target of potentiators such as ivacaftor, not the deltaF508 mechanism.
deltaF508 is an in-frame deletion, not a stop codon.
CF reduces, not increases, channel activity.

items.rationale: Potentiators such as ivacaftor hold the CFTR channel gate open so chloride flows; correctors such as lumacaftor and tezacaftor help the protein fold and reach the cell surface.

Ivacaftor does not block ENaC.

items.stem: Men with cystic fibrosis are usually infertile because of which abnormality?
items.rationale: Male infertility in cystic fibrosis results from absence of the vas deferens, while spermatogenesis may be unaffected.
expl: Hypogonadism is not the usual cause.
Immotile sperm from dynein defects is Kartagener syndrome.
Spermatogenesis may be unaffected.

items.stem: Laboratory tests that measure glucose by its reducing property depend on which structural feature of the sugar?
options: The carbon next to the last carbon

expl: The penultimate carbon determines D or L configuration, not reducing ability.
A glycosidic bond at the anomeric carbon removes, rather than creates, reducing ability.
Hydroxyl groups do not make a sugar reducing.

Troponin binding cannot precede calcium release.

items.rationale: Hypomagnesemia (below 1.0 mEq/L) causes hypokalemia and hypocalcemia, which correct only after magnesium is replaced.
expl: Sodium does not cause refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia.
Phosphate deficiency causes bone loss and weakness.
Bicarbonate is not the missing ion.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A patient with metabolic acidosis has HCO3- of 12 mEq/L and PaCO2 of 26 mm Hg. How should the respiratory response be interpreted?
items.rationale: By the Winters formula, predicted PCO2 = 1.5 x 12 + 8 = 26, plus or minus 2; the measured 26 mm Hg is appropriate compensation.
expl: Respiratory acidosis would give a PCO2 above 28.
Respiratory alkalosis would give a PCO2 below 24.
The primary process is metabolic acidosis.

items.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has HCO3- of 10 mEq/L and PaCO2 of 35 mm Hg. What does the PaCO2 indicate?
items.rationale: Predicted PCO2 = 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23, plus or minus 2; a measured PCO2 above the prediction indicates a concomitant respiratory acidosis.
expl: Respiratory alkalosis would give a PCO2 below prediction.

Appropriate compensation would give about 21 to 25 mm Hg.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: What is the immediate compensatory response to metabolic acidosis?
items.rationale: Metabolic acidosis is compensated immediately by hyperventilation, which lowers PCO2; metabolic alkalosis is compensated by hypoventilation.
expl: Bicarbonate excretion would worsen acidosis.
Hypoventilation compensates metabolic alkalosis.
Chloride retention is not the compensation.

expl: Current diuretic use raises urine chloride.
Bartter syndrome gives urine chloride above 20.

items.stem: A dehydrated 1-year-old with watery diarrhea needs intravenous fluid. Which fluid expands the extracellular volume least for the same infused volume?
items.rationale: Once the dextrose is metabolized, 5% dextrose in water provides free water that distributes through total body water, so only a small fraction stays extracellular; isotonic saline solutions stay in the extracellular space.
expl: Lactated Ringer solution is isotonic and remains extracellular.
Isotonic saline remains extracellular.
Dextrose in saline leaves isotonic saline in the extracellular space.

options: The left pupil constricts while the right dilates
The left pupil dilates while the right constricts
items.rationale: A one-sided lesion of the afferent limb (retina or optic nerve) causes a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil): swinging the light from the normal to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate instead of constricting.

Further constriction occurs when the light moves to a normal eye.
The consensual reflex keeps the two pupils moving together.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A patient has a complete left oculomotor nerve palsy. A light is shone into the left eye. Which pupillary response follows?
options: The left pupil constricts; the right does not
The right pupil constricts; the left does not
items.rationale: Light in either eye signals via CN II to the pretectal nuclei, which activate both Edinger-Westphal nuclei; the afferent limb is intact, so the right pupil constricts consensually, while the left pupil cannot constrict because its efferent CN III is damaged.
expl: The damaged left efferent limb prevents equal constriction.
The left sphincter pupillae has lost its CN III supply.
The intact afferent limb still drives the right pupil.

items.stem: The first-order sympathetic neuron for pupillary dilation runs from the hypothalamus to which site?
items.rationale: Pupillary dilation is sympathetic: the first neuron runs from the hypothalamus to the ciliospinal center of Budge (C8-T2), the second exits at T1 to the superior cervical ganglion, and the third travels with the internal carotid artery to the long ciliary nerves.
expl: The superior cervical ganglion holds the third-order neuron cell bodies.
The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic relay.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is parasympathetic and drives constriction.

items.stem: After tropicamide eye drops, a patient cannot focus on near print. Blockade of which muscarinic effect explains this?
items.rationale: M3 receptors mediate ciliary muscle contraction (accommodation) and sphincter pupillae contraction (miosis); an antimuscarinic such as tropicamide causes cycloplegia, so near focus fails, along with mydriasis.
expl: Aqueous secretion does not determine near focus.
The dilator pupillae is driven by alpha-1 receptors.
Blocking sphincter contraction explains the dilated pupil, while near focus depends on the ciliary muscle.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: What is the first molecular event when light strikes rhodopsin?
options: Isomerization of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal
Isomerization of all-trans retinal to 11-cis retinal
Direct activation of phosphodiesterase by opsin
items.rationale: Rhodopsin is 11-cis retinal bound to opsin; light converts 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal, which dissociates from opsin and starts the cascade that lowers cGMP and closes cation channels.
expl: Light closes cGMP-gated cation channels as cGMP falls.
Conversion back to 11-cis retinal is the regeneration step of the visual cycle.
Activated rhodopsin acts through transducin, which then activates phosphodiesterase.

options: Exposure to ultraviolet light for 10 minutes
Immersion in boiling water for 5 minutes

Alcohol disinfects vegetative cells but does not kill spores, which resist chemicals.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A 58-year-old man with pyelonephritis becomes hypotensive and begins oozing from venipuncture sites. Blood cultures grow a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Which host interaction initiates his release of interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor?
options: Lipid A binding the CD14–TLR4 complex on macrophages
Protein A binding the Fc region of IgG
Superantigen cross-linking of MHC class II and T-cell receptors
Heat-labile toxin activation of enterocyte adenylate cyclase
items.rationale: Lipid A of the gram-negative outer membrane activates macrophages through TLR4/CD14, releasing IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α; endotoxin also activates complement and tissue factor, which explains the hypotension and the bleeding of disseminated intravascular coagulation.
expl: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus surface protein that blocks opsonization; it does not trigger macrophage cytokine release in this infection.
Superantigens are exotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, not of a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.
Heat-labile toxin raises cAMP in enterocytes and causes watery diarrhea, not septic shock with coagulopathy.

items.stem: A 19-year-old military recruit has a week of dry cough and low-grade fever. The chest radiograph looks worse than his examination, and sputum Gram stain shows no organisms. Why would a cephalosporin fail against the likely pathogen?
options: The organism's cell wall is rich in mycolic acid
The organism lives only within macrophage phagosomes
The organism produces an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase
The organism has no peptidoglycan cell wall
items.rationale: Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical pneumonia in young adults in closed settings. It has no cell wall, so beta-lactams have no target and it is not seen on Gram stain; macrolides, doxycycline, or fluoroquinolones are used.
expl: Mycolic acid characterizes mycobacteria; Mycoplasma has a sterol-containing membrane instead.
Mycoplasma is an extracellular surface parasite of respiratory epithelium, not an obligate phagosome dweller.
Resistance here is from a missing target, not an enzyme that destroys the drug.

The agent's nucleic acid is shielded by a capsid

To block the organism's IgA protease on mucosa
To neutralize a diphtheria-like exotoxin made by the organism

expl: The Hib conjugate vaccine is injected, not given orally.
The carrier protein does not inhibit bacterial IgA protease.
Haemophilus influenzae type b does not make a diphtheria-like toxin; the toxoid serves only as a protein carrier.

A toxin already formed in the food was ingested

Mucosal invasion takes longer and causes fever and bloody stool, which these diners lack.
Blocked acetylcholine release is botulism, which causes descending paralysis rather than early vomiting alone.

items.stem: Clostridium, Bacteroides, and Fusobacterium are damaged by exposure to air. Which missing enzymes explain this?
items.rationale: Anaerobes lack catalase and/or superoxide dismutase, so reactive oxygen species damage them.
expl: Urease and lipase have no antioxidant role.
Beta-lactamase inactivates beta-lactam drugs and IgA protease cleaves IgA; neither affects oxygen tolerance.
Coagulase and hyaluronidase are tissue-acting virulence enzymes; neither protects against reactive oxygen species.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Purified genomic nucleic acid, without any viral proteins, is introduced into permissive cells. Which genome type can start an infection on its own?
items.rationale: Positive-sense RNA acts directly as messenger RNA, so its naked genome is infectious. Negative-sense and double-stranded RNA genomes need the RNA polymerase carried in the virion, and poxvirus DNA needs virion enzymes as well.
expl: Negative-sense RNA must first be transcribed by the polymerase packaged in the virion.
Double-stranded RNA viruses also lack the required polymerase when stripped of their proteins.
Poxviruses replicate in the cytoplasm with virion enzymes, so their naked DNA is an exception among DNA viruses.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A new influenza A strain carrying gene segments from avian, swine, and human viruses spreads worldwide, and few people have protective antibodies. Which property of the virus made this strain possible?
options: A segmented genome that allows reassortment
Point mutations from an error-prone polymerase
Integration of a DNA copy into host chromosomes
Coating of its genome by another virus's proteins
items.rationale: Influenza has a segmented genome. When one cell is infected by two different segmented viruses, segments reassort (antigenic shift), producing a novel strain that can cause a pandemic; shift is more dangerous than gradual drift.
expl: Point mutations cause antigenic drift, which produces seasonal epidemics, not a strain with segments from three species.
Influenza does not integrate into the host genome; integration is a retrovirus feature.
Phenotypic mixing changes the coat of one generation only and does not create a new genome.

items.stem: Brain tissue from a patient who died of encephalitis weeks after a dog bite shows eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in Purkinje cells and hippocampal neurons. What are these inclusions called?

expl: Cowdry type A bodies are intranuclear inclusions of herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses.
Lewy bodies are alpha-synuclein inclusions of Parkinson disease.
Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in viral hepatitis and yellow fever.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A man bitten on the hand by a stray dog develops agitation and hydrophobia only after several weeks. How did the virus travel from the bite to the brain?
items.rationale: Rabies virus binds acetylcholine receptors at the bite site and migrates retrogradely up nerve axons on dynein motors, which explains the long incubation and why bites closer to the head shorten it.
expl: Rabies does not reach the brain through the bloodstream.
Lymphatic spread is not the route of rabies to the brain.
Kinesin moves cargo anterogradely, away from the cell body, the wrong direction for reaching the CNS.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A 10-year-old is bitten on the calf by an unvaccinated stray dog; the bite breaks the skin and bleeds. After thorough wound washing, which prophylaxis is indicated?
options: Tetanus toxoid and wound care only
items.rationale: Rabies postexposure prophylaxis is wound cleaning plus immunization with killed vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin; the immunoglobulin gives immediate passive protection while the vaccine induces active immunity.
expl: Tetanus prophylaxis may also be needed, but it gives no protection against rabies.
Immunoglobulin alone gives only temporary protection without lasting active immunity.
Vaccine alone leaves the child unprotected until antibodies develop after a high-risk bite.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis B starts tenofovir, a nucleotide analog also used against HIV. Why is this antiretroviral drug active against a DNA virus?
options: HBV copies an RNA intermediate into DNA with reverse transcriptase
HBV DNA polymerase is identical to human DNA polymerase
HBV packages a diploid RNA genome like HIV
HBV integrates its genome using a retroviral integrase
items.rationale: Hepatitis B virus is a partially double-stranded DNA virus that is not a retrovirus, but its polymerase has reverse transcriptase activity: it makes DNA from a pregenomic RNA, which nucleotide analogs such as tenofovir inhibit.
expl: If the viral polymerase were identical to the host enzyme, the drug could not act selectively.
HBV virions contain DNA, not a diploid RNA genome.
HBV does not depend on a retroviral integrase; integrase inhibitors are not HBV therapy.

options: Villous destruction that reduces sodium absorption
Granulomatous inflammation of the terminal ileum
Invasion of colonic mucosa, causing bloody stools
An A-B toxin that raises enterocyte cAMP
items.rationale: Rotavirus, a segmented double-stranded RNA reovirus, destroys intestinal villi; villous atrophy reduces sodium absorption and causes loss of potassium, giving watery diarrhea.

Colonic invasion with bloody stools describes Shigella or enteroinvasive organisms.
A-B toxins that raise cAMP describe cholera toxin and enterotoxigenic E. coli, not rotavirus.

items.stem: A child with sickle cell disease develops sudden severe anemia with almost no reticulocytes. His sister recently had a slapped-cheek rash. How does the responsible virus cause the anemia?
options: It induces cold agglutinins against red cells
It infects erythroid progenitors bearing the P antigen
It lyses mature red cells in the circulation
items.rationale: Parvovirus B19 uses the P antigen on red cell precursors as its receptor and halts erythropoiesis; in sickle cell disease, whose red cells survive briefly, this produces an aplastic crisis with reticulocytopenia.
expl: Parvovirus does not act on renal erythropoietin production.
Cold agglutinin hemolysis is linked to Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Epstein-Barr virus, and it would show reticulocytosis.
Circulating red cell lysis would raise, not abolish, the reticulocyte count.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A cervical biopsy shows high-grade squamous dysplasia with HPV-16. Which viral gene products drive the dysplasia, and how?
options: L1, by activating the RAS pathway
E2, by amplifying the MYC gene
E6 and E7, by inhibiting p53 and Rb
L2, by inhibiting the APC protein
items.rationale: HPV-16 and HPV-18 produce E6, which inhibits p53, and E7, which inhibits Rb; loss of these tumor suppressors drives dysplasia and carcinoma.
expl: L1 is the major capsid protein used in the vaccine; it is not an oncoprotein.
E2 regulates viral transcription; it is not the protein that inactivates tumor suppressors.
L2 is a minor capsid protein with no role in inhibiting APC.

Core antigen to build its capsid

Low IgG, IgA, and IgM with absent B cells
Normal immunoglobulins with low C3 and C4
High IgM with low IgG and IgA

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Ten days after receiving equine antivenom for a snakebite, a farmer develops fever, urticarial rash, arthralgia, and proteinuria, with low serum complement. What is the mechanism?
options: Deposition of antibody–foreign protein complexes in tissues
Cross-linking of IgE on sensitized mast cells
Antibody binding to fixed antigens on cell surfaces
Cytokine release by sensitized T lymphocytes
items.rationale: Serum sickness is the prototypic immune complex (type III) disease: antibodies form against foreign proteins over 1 to 2 weeks, and the complexes deposit in tissues and consume complement.
expl: IgE cross-linking is type I hypersensitivity, which occurs within minutes.
Antibody against fixed cell-surface antigens is type II hypersensitivity.
Cytokine release by sensitized T cells is type IV hypersensitivity, which involves no antibodies or complement consumption.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Minutes after the vascular anastomosis of a kidney transplant is completed, the graft becomes mottled and cyanotic. What caused this?
options: Preformed recipient antibodies against donor antigens
Donor T cells attacking recipient tissues
Recipient CD8 T cells sensitized over weeks
Slow intimal fibrosis of graft arteries
items.rationale: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes when pre-existing recipient antibodies react with donor antigens and activate complement (type II hypersensitivity), causing widespread graft thrombosis.
expl: Donor T cells attacking the host is graft-versus-host disease, seen mainly after bone marrow transplant.
Sensitized recipient T cells cause acute cellular rejection weeks later.
Intimal fibrosis is chronic rejection, which develops over months to years.

items.stem: A child bitten by a dog receives rabies immunoglobulin into the wound. What type of immunity does the immunoglobulin provide?
items.rationale: Passive immunity comes from receiving preformed antibodies; it is rapid but short-lived. Injected immunoglobulin is artificially acquired, unlike maternal IgG or breast-milk IgA.

Active immunity requires exposure to antigen, as with the rabies vaccine.

items.stem: A farmworker who walks barefoot has fatigue and pallor; his smear shows microcytic, hypochromic red cells, and his stool has thin-shelled oval eggs. How does the parasite cause his anemia?
options: Adult worms compete for vitamin B12 in the ileum
Eggs cause bleeding through the bladder wall
Larvae destroy red cells as they pass the lungs
Adult worms suck blood from the intestinal wall
items.rationale: Hookworms (Ancylostoma and Necator) attach to the intestinal wall and suck blood, causing chronic blood loss and microcytic iron deficiency anemia.
expl: Competition for vitamin B12 is the mechanism of Diphyllobothrium latum and causes macrocytic anemia.
Bladder bleeding from eggs is Schistosoma haematobium.
Lung migration causes transient pneumonitis, not hemolysis.

items.stem: A 60-year-old farmer from Leyte on high-dose prednisone for COPD develops gram-negative bacteremia, diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and abdominal pain. His stool contains larvae. Which feature of the parasite explains how severe this became?
options: Adult worms migrating up the bile duct
Eggs that need weeks in soil before they infect
items.rationale: Strongyloides stercoralis completes its life cycle within the host (autoinfection). Immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids, accelerates autoinfection into hyperinfection, and migrating larvae carry gut bacteria into the blood.
expl: Biliary migration is an Ascaris complication and does not cause gram-negative bacteremia with pulmonary infiltrates.
Encystment in striated muscle is Trichinella spiralis.
Soil maturation of eggs limits worm burden in hookworm and Ascaris; it does not explain amplification within one host.

options: Anaphylaxis to antigens spilled from the cyst
Embolism of daughter cysts to the lungs
Hemorrhage from an injured portal vein
Septic shock from cyst bacterial superinfection
items.rationale: Echinococcus granulosus forms hydatid cysts with eggshell calcification, mostly in the liver and lungs; cyst rupture can cause anaphylaxis.
expl: Spilled protoscolices seed new cysts, but daughter-cyst embolism does not produce urticaria and wheezing.
Hemorrhage causes hypotension without wheezing or urticaria.
Septic shock would not cause wheezing and urticaria within moments of drainage.

items.rationale: Entamoeba histolytica causes dysentery and liver abscess with anchovy-paste fluid. Metronidazole treats tissue disease, and a luminal agent such as paromomycin or iodoquinol clears intestinal cysts.
expl: Praziquantel and ivermectin treat helminths, not protozoa.
Antibacterial regimens treat pyogenic abscesses but do not eradicate amebae.
Benzimidazoles and praziquantel are anthelmintics with no role in amebiasis.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A man with HIV and a CD4 count of 60 cells/mm3 develops headache and right hemiparesis. MRI shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which prophylaxis would most likely have prevented this?
items.rationale: Toxoplasma reactivation in AIDS causes brain abscesses seen as multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole) is given when the CD4 count is below 100 cells/mm3.
expl: Fluconazole is not routine primary prophylaxis and has no activity against Toxoplasma.
Azithromycin prevents Mycobacterium avium complex disease, not toxoplasmosis.
Isoniazid treats latent tuberculosis and has no activity against Toxoplasma.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A soldier treated for malaria in Palawan relapses 6 months later without new exposure. The smear shows enlarged infected red cells with Schüffner stippling. Which drug should have been added to his first treatment to prevent this relapse?
items.rationale: Plasmodium vivax and ovale leave dormant hypnozoites in the liver that cause relapse; primaquine is added to target them.
expl: Artesunate is a rapid blood schizonticide for severe malaria; it does not clear hypnozoites.
Doxycycline treats or prevents blood-stage infection and does not eradicate liver hypnozoites.
Chloroquine kills blood-stage parasites but not hypnozoites.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Before giving primaquine for Plasmodium vivax infection, which test should be done?
items.rationale: Primaquine is an oxidizing drug; people with G6PD deficiency have poor red cell defense against oxidants and can develop hemolytic anemia.
expl: Hemoglobin electrophoresis detects hemoglobinopathies, which do not predict primaquine hemolysis.
The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test detects antibody-mediated hemolysis, not oxidant susceptibility.
Ferritin measures iron stores, which do not affect primaquine safety.

Up the facial nerve by retrograde transport
Through the blood after lung infection
By extension from an infected paranasal sinus

items.stem: A 16-year-old using tampons during menses develops fever, hypotension, diffuse erythroderma, and later desquamation of the palms. Blood cultures are negative. How does the responsible toxin cause shock?
options: It cleaves SNARE proteins at peripheral nerve terminals
It inserts pores into the membranes of host cells
It links T-cell receptors to MHC class II outside the peptide groove
It ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2 in host cells
items.rationale: Toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 of Staphylococcus aureus is a superantigen: it cross-links the T-cell receptor beta region to MHC class II outside the antigen-binding site, activating many T cells and releasing massive cytokines.
expl: SNARE cleavage is the action of tetanus and botulinum toxins.
Pore-forming toxins such as streptolysin O lyse cells; they are not superantigens.
ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2 is the action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.

items.rationale: Staphylococcus aureus toxins cause scalded skin syndrome (exfoliative toxin), toxic shock (TSST-1), and food poisoning (heat-stable enterotoxin); exfoliative toxin splits the superficial epidermis without mucosal involvement.

Streptolysin O is a hemolysin that induces ASO antibodies; it does not split the epidermis.

items.stem: Three weeks after a dental extraction, a man with mitral valve prolapse has low-grade fever, a new murmur, and splinter hemorrhages. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant streptococci. Which bacterial product allowed them to colonize the valve?
options: IgA protease that cleaves mucosal antibody
A capsule that resists complement opsonization
items.rationale: Viridans streptococci such as S. sanguinis make dextrans that bind to fibrin-platelet aggregates on damaged heart valves, causing subacute infective endocarditis after dental procedures.
expl: IgA protease helps mucosal colonization by organisms such as S. pneumoniae; it does not anchor bacteria to valves.
Capsule-mediated complement resistance characterizes S. pneumoniae, which is optochin sensitive.
M protein is the antiphagocytic protein of Streptococcus pyogenes, which is beta-hemolytic.

items.stem: Two weeks after impetigo, a 7-year-old develops cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and hypertension. Serum C3 is low. Which mechanism explains the kidney injury?
options: Antibodies to the glomerular basement membrane
Direct bacterial invasion of the glomeruli
Immune complexes deposited in the glomeruli
items.rationale: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III hypersensitivity: immune complexes form after group A streptococcal infection, deposit in glomeruli, and activate complement, lowering C3.
expl: Streptococcal toxins do not cause this delayed nephritic syndrome.
Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies cause Goodpasture syndrome, a type II reaction with normal complement.
The infection is in the skin; the kidney injury is immune mediated, not bacterial invasion.

items.stem: When is a pregnant patient screened for group B streptococcal colonization, and what follows a positive culture?
options: At the first visit; oral amoxicillin for 7 days
At 28 weeks; one dose of benzathine penicillin
At 35 to 37 weeks; intrapartum penicillin or ampicillin
At delivery; ceftriaxone given to the newborn
items.rationale: Pregnant patients are screened at 35 to 37 weeks with rectal and vaginal swabs; those with a positive culture receive intrapartum penicillin or ampicillin prophylaxis.
expl: Early screening misses later colonization, and antepartum oral antibiotics do not prevent neonatal infection.
Screening is not done at 28 weeks, and a single antepartum dose does not cover labor.
Prophylaxis is given to the mother during labor, not to the newborn after delivery.

items.stem: A farmer with a deep puncture wound develops trismus, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonos. The toxin produces spastic paralysis by blocking release of which neurotransmitters, from which cells?
options: GABA and glycine from Renshaw cells
items.rationale: Tetanospasmin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters GABA and glycine from Renshaw cells in the spinal cord, producing spastic paralysis, trismus, and opisthotonos.
expl: Dopamine loss in the substantia nigra is Parkinson disease.
Tetanus toxin does not act on cortical glutamate release.
Blocking acetylcholine release at motor terminals is botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid paralysis.

items.stem: A 3-month-old who was fed honey develops constipation, a weak cry, poor suck, and descending flaccid weakness. How was the infant exposed to the toxin?
options: Ingested spores germinated and made toxin in the gut
Toxin crossed the placenta before delivery
Preformed toxin in the honey was absorbed
Toxin entered through a contaminated skin wound
items.rationale: Infant botulism is caused by ingestion of spores, for example from soil or raw honey; the toxin is produced in vivo, unlike adult foodborne botulism from preformed toxin.
expl: Botulinum toxin is not transferred across the placenta.
Ingesting preformed toxin is the mechanism of foodborne botulism, typically from improperly canned food.
Wound botulism follows contamination of a wound, which this infant does not have.

items.stem: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus resists nearly all beta-lactam drugs. What is the basis of this resistance?
options: Plasmid-encoded beta-lactamase that hydrolyzes the drug
Efflux pumps that export the drug from the cell
Altered penicillin-binding proteins encoded by mecA
Loss of outer-membrane porins that admit the drug
items.rationale: MRSA resistance is due to altered penicillin-binding proteins conferred by the mecA gene, so beta-lactams cannot bind their target.
expl: Penicillinase-stable drugs such as methicillin resist beta-lactamase; MRSA resistance is not enzymatic.
Efflux is not the mechanism of methicillin resistance.
Staphylococci are gram-positive and have no outer membrane or porins.

expl: Exfoliative toxin causes scalded skin syndrome.

TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome through superantigen activity.

items.stem: Staphylococci, streptococci, and enteric gram-negative rods use oxygen when available but switch to fermentation without it. What are such bacteria called?
items.rationale: Facultative anaerobes use oxygen when present but also use fermentation and other oxygen-independent pathways; examples are streptococci, staphylococci, and enteric gram-negative bacteria.
expl: Microaerophiles need reduced oxygen concentrations, as Campylobacter does.
Obligate aerobes need oxygen and cannot ferment to survive without it.
Obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate oxygen because they lack catalase or superoxide dismutase.

items.stem: Which property distinguishes bacterial exotoxins from endotoxin?
options: They form part of the outer membrane
They are released mainly when cells lyse
They are made of lipid A and polysaccharide
They can be inactivated into toxoid vaccines
items.rationale: Exotoxins are secreted polypeptides that induce high-titer antitoxins and can be converted into toxoid vaccines; endotoxin is poorly antigenic and has no toxoid vaccine.
expl: Endotoxin is the outer-membrane component; exotoxins are secreted.
Release on cell lysis characterizes endotoxin.
Lipid A with polysaccharide is lipopolysaccharide, the endotoxin.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Most exotoxins are destroyed rapidly at 60 °C. Which of these is an exception?
items.rationale: Exotoxins are generally destroyed rapidly at 60 °C, except staphylococcal enterotoxin, E. coli heat-stable toxin, and the B. cereus emetic toxin; reheating food therefore does not prevent staphylococcal food poisoning.
expl: Diphtheria toxin is heat labile.
Tetanospasmin is heat labile like most exotoxins.
Botulinum toxin is destroyed by adequate heating, which is why boiling home-canned food is protective.

expl: Cystine stones result from an inherited transport defect.

Uric acid stones form in acidic urine, the opposite of what urease produces.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A small gram-negative coccobacillus from a child's cerebrospinal fluid grows on chocolate agar. On blood agar it grows only around colonies of Staphylococcus aureus. Why does it grow there?
options: Staphylococci lower the local oxygen tension
Staphylococci secrete siderophores that supply iron
items.rationale: Haemophilus influenzae needs factors V (NAD+) and X (hematin), supplied by chocolate agar. On blood agar, S. aureus lyses red cells and releases factor V, so Haemophilus grows as satellite colonies.
expl: Haemophilus is not an anaerobe that needs reduced oxygen.
Iron siderophores do not supply factor V, the missing growth requirement.
The limiting factor is NAD+, not inhibitory serum proteins.

options: They prolong fecal excretion of the organism
Antibiotics provoke Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions in salmonellosis
Antibiotics trigger hemolytic-uremic syndrome in Salmonella infection
Salmonella is resistant to all oral antibiotics

Many Salmonella strains are susceptible; resistance is not the reason for withholding treatment.

It survives on dry surfaces as spores
It is carried by household pets
It spreads mainly by respiratory droplets

expl: Shigella does not form spores.

Shigella spreads by the fecal-oral route, not by droplets.

Strong cell-mediated immunity with a Th1 response
Weak cell-mediated immunity with a Th2 response

expl: Leprosy patients have B cells; antibody does not control the infection.
Complement deficiency is not the basis of lepromatous leprosy.
Strong Th1 immunity produces the limited tuberculoid form with few bacilli.

Oxygen tension does not explain the predilection for skin and superficial nerves.

items.stem: Why is rifampin never used alone to treat active tuberculosis?
options: It is excreted before it can reach the lungs
It has no activity against intracellular bacilli
RNA polymerase mutations quickly produce resistance
It acts only on dormant, nonreplicating bacilli
items.rationale: Rifampin inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase; mutations in the RNA polymerase gene cause resistance, and monotherapy rapidly selects resistant bacilli.
expl: Rifampin reaches the lungs and is effective there.
Rifampin is active against intracellular and extracellular bacilli.
Rifampin acts on replicating bacilli, not only dormant ones.

items.stem: Isoniazid-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates often carry katG mutations. Why do these mutations cause resistance?
options: The drug is pumped out by efflux transporters
The cell wall becomes impermeable to the drug
The drug is no longer converted to its active form
items.rationale: Isoniazid is a prodrug: bacterial catalase-peroxidase encoded by katG converts it to its active form, which inhibits mycolic acid synthesis. Loss of katG activity prevents activation.
expl: Efflux is not the mechanism linked to katG mutations.
Arabinosyltransferase is the ethambutol target.
katG mutations affect drug activation, not permeability.

Meropenem is a carbapenem with some cross-reactivity risk.

items.rationale: HIV binds CD4 and a coreceptor, CCR5 on macrophages early in infection or CXCR4 on T cells later. Homozygous CCR5 mutation confers immunity; heterozygous mutation slows the course.

Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis without black vomitus and hemorrhagic fever.

Congenital toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and calcifications.

Shearing of red cells by microthrombi

items.stem: A farmer from northern Luzon who often eats raw freshwater fish has months of watery diarrhea, weight loss, and edema. Stool contains eggs, larvae, and adults of Capillaria philippinensis. Which feature of this nematode explains the very large worm burden?
options: Repeated skin penetration by soil-dwelling larvae
Encystment of larvae within striated muscle
Asexual budding of larval cysts in the liver
Autoinfection that multiplies worms inside the host
items.rationale: A few parasites, including Strongyloides stercoralis, Capillaria philippinensis, and Hymenolepis nana, can increase in number within one host through autoinfection, so untreated infection worsens without new exposure.
expl: Skin penetration from soil is the route of hookworm and Strongyloides, not fish-borne Capillaria.
Muscle encystment is a feature of Trichinella.
Budding larval cysts describe Echinococcus hydatid disease.

items.stem: In most endemic areas, when should blood be drawn to detect Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae?
options: During an attack of acute lymphangitis
Early morning, after an overnight fast
At midday, when the patient is active
items.rationale: Blood samples for microfilariae must be obtained when microfilaremia peaks, which is at night in most endemic areas (during the day in many Pacific islands).
expl: Acute lymphangitis does not mark the peak of circulating microfilariae.
Fasting has no effect on microfilarial periodicity.
In most endemic areas daytime blood misses nocturnally periodic microfilariae.

items.stem: A man who returned from a forested area of Palawan has Plasmodium falciparum malaria with impaired consciousness and 8% parasitemia. Which treatment is indicated?
items.rationale: Life-threatening malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate or quinine (with G6PD testing where relevant); oral regimens are for uncomplicated disease.
expl: Doxycycline is a slow partner drug, never sole therapy for severe malaria.
Primaquine targets liver hypnozoites and gametocytes, not severe blood-stage disease.
Oral chloroquine is for uncomplicated, chloroquine-sensitive malaria and is too slow and unreliable here.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A newborn has chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications. Which maternal exposure during pregnancy is the most common source of this infection?
options: Contact with a toddler's urine and saliva
Eating undercooked meat with tissue cysts
Sexual contact with an infected partner
items.rationale: Congenital toxoplasmosis causes the triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications. Infection is most commonly from cysts in meat, also from oocysts in cat feces, and the parasite crosses the placenta.
expl: Toddler urine and saliva transmit cytomegalovirus, which causes periventricular calcifications.
Unpasteurized milk transmits Listeria and Brucella.
Sexual transmission fits syphilis or HSV, not toxoplasmosis.

items.stem: Why are pregnant patients advised to avoid handling cat litter?
options: Cat feces may carry Salmonella typhi
Litter dust may carry Histoplasma spores
Cat feces may carry Listeria bacteria
Cat feces may carry Toxoplasma oocysts

expl: Salmonella typhi has a human-only reservoir.
Histoplasma is associated with bird and bat droppings, not cat litter.
Listeria comes from unpasteurized dairy and deli meats.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Why has no vaccine against hepatitis C virus been developed?
options: Its envelope proteins vary because replication lacks proofreading
It replicates only within circulating lymphocytes
It causes infection without any antibody response
It is a DNA virus that integrates into hepatocyte DNA
items.rationale: HCV lacks 3'-5' exonuclease activity, so its replication has no proofreading; the resulting antigenic variation of its envelope proteins has defeated vaccine development.
expl: HCV replicates in hepatocytes, not mainly in lymphocytes.
Infection induces antibodies, but they do not protect against the variant envelope.
HCV is an RNA flavivirus and does not integrate into host DNA.

items.stem: During a waterborne outbreak after a typhoon, a woman in her third trimester develops acute hepatitis. Infection with which virus carries a high mortality in her?
items.rationale: Hepatitis E is transmitted fecal-orally, especially through water, and causes fulminant hepatitis with high mortality in pregnant patients.
expl: Hepatitis B is spread parenterally, sexually, and perinatally, not by water.
Hepatitis C is blood-borne and not transmitted by contaminated water.
Hepatitis A is also fecal-oral but has a good prognosis and is not especially lethal in pregnancy.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A man with chronic hepatitis B acquires hepatitis D through shared needles. How does the prognosis of this superinfection compare with simultaneous HBV-HDV coinfection?
options: Better, because HDV clears the HBV infection
Same, because HDV needs no help from HBV
Better, because prior HBV immunity limits HDV
Worse, with more severe liver disease
items.rationale: HDV is a defective virus that needs the HBsAg coat; superinfection of a chronic HBV carrier carries a worse prognosis than coinfection.
expl: HDV does not cure HBV; superinfection worsens liver disease.
HDV depends on HBV for its coat and cannot spread without it.
Chronic HBV supplies HBsAg, so it enables rather than limits HDV.

The window period shows IgM anti-HBc without HBsAg or anti-HBs.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A 10-day-old has fever, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle. Cerebrospinal fluid shows neutrophils, high protein, and low glucose. Which group of pathogens must empiric therapy cover?
options: S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and Hib
Enteroviruses, HSV-2, and West Nile virus
Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria
items.rationale: In newborns up to 6 months, meningitis is most commonly caused by group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria; the CSF picture is bacterial.
expl: Pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Hib are the main causes in older infants and children.
These viral causes produce lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
Fungal and tuberculous meningitis are subacute and seen mainly in immunocompromised hosts.

expl: Cryptococcal meningitis gives lymphocytes with low glucose and high pressure, usually in immunocompromised hosts.
Bacterial meningitis gives neutrophils and low glucose.
Tuberculous meningitis gives lymphocytes with low glucose and high pressure.

items.rationale: Single brain abscesses arise from contiguous sites: sinusitis or dental infection spreads to the frontal lobe, and otitis media or mastoiditis to the temporal lobe and cerebellum. Multiple abscesses usually come from bacteremia.

Otitis media and mastoiditis cause temporal lobe or cerebellar abscesses.
Bacteremia usually produces multiple abscesses.

options: Ganciclovir, which uses the same viral kinase
Valacyclovir, which reaches higher drug levels
Foscarnet, which needs no viral kinase activation

They neutralize virus as antibodies do

expl: Interferons do not act by activating complement.
Interferons act on host cells, not on free virions.
Interferons are cytokines, not antibodies.

items.stem: Why does the 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) give weak, short-lived protection and need boosters?
options: Maternal IgA neutralizes the vaccine antigens
Recipients lack complement to process them
They elicit T-independent responses without memory
Polysaccharides are destroyed by gastric acid
items.rationale: Thymus-independent antigens, which lack a peptide component, cannot recruit helper T cells, so they give poor class switching and memory; vaccines such as the PPSV23 capsular polysaccharide often need boosters and adjuvants.
expl: Maternal IgA does not neutralize injected vaccine antigens.
Complement deficiency is not the reason for the weak response.
PPSV23 is injected, so gastric acid is irrelevant.

options: Point mutations in HA and NA cause antigenic drift
The virus integrates into host DNA

Influenza does not integrate into host DNA.

items.stem: A man with AIDS has red-purple vascular papules on the skin. Biopsy shows proliferating capillaries with neutrophils and organisms visible on silver stain. Which organism is responsible?
items.rationale: Bartonella causes cat scratch disease and, in immunocompromised hosts, bacillary angiomatosis; the organisms take up silver stain.
expl: Pseudomonas causes ecthyma gangrenosum, a necrotic lesion, not angiomatous papules.
Treponema causes syphilitic lesions, not vascular proliferations with neutrophils.
HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, with spindle cells and lymphocytes rather than neutrophils and bacteria.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A man has gonococcal urethritis on Gram stain, and his chlamydia test result will not be available for several days. Which regimen is appropriate now?
items.rationale: Gonorrhea is treated with a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone; if chlamydial coinfection is not excluded by molecular testing, doxycycline is added.
expl: Ceftriaxone alone leaves possible chlamydial coinfection untreated.
Azithromycin alone is not adequate gonococcal therapy.
Ciprofloxacin resistance is common, and metronidazole does not cover chlamydia.

items.stem: A 10-day-old has watery-to-mucopurulent conjunctivitis. His mother had untreated cervicitis. Which organism is most likely, given the timing?
items.rationale: Chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis appears 1 to 2 weeks after birth, whereas gonococcal conjunctivitis appears 2 to 5 days after birth.
expl: Gonococcal conjunctivitis appears within 2 to 5 days, with copious purulent discharge.
S. epidermidis is a skin commensal, not a classic cause of neonatal conjunctivitis.
Neonatal HSV usually causes vesicles or keratitis and systemic illness rather than this picture.

items.stem: Which antituberculous drug is most active at acidic pH, such as inside host phagolysosomes?
items.rationale: Pyrazinamide works best at acidic pH, as in host phagolysosomes, which is why it helps kill intracellular bacilli early in therapy.
expl: Rifampin inhibits RNA polymerase regardless of pH.
Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyltransferase.
Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis and is not defined by acid activation.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Why does Pseudomonas aeruginosa establish chronic lung infection in patients with cystic fibrosis?
options: Its mucoid polysaccharide forms a biofilm
It survives only within alveolar macrophages
It cleaves secretory IgA on the airway
items.rationale: Pseudomonas's mucoid polysaccharide capsule may contribute to chronic pneumonia in cystic fibrosis through biofilm formation.
expl: Pseudomonas is not an obligate intracellular organism.
IgA protease is a feature of Neisseria, Haemophilus, and S. pneumoniae.
Pseudomonas exotoxin A inhibits protein synthesis but is not a neurotoxin and does not explain persistence.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Shiga toxin of Shigella dysenteriae damages the intestinal mucosa by which action?
options: Permanently activating Gs to raise cellular cAMP
Cleaving SNARE proteins needed for vesicle fusion
Removing adenine from rRNA, inactivating the 60S ribosome
ADP-ribosylating elongation factor 2 in host cells
items.rationale: Shiga toxin inactivates the 60S ribosome by removing adenine from rRNA, killing cells and causing dysentery; in EHEC it also causes hemolytic-uremic syndrome.
expl: Gs activation is the action of cholera toxin and heat-labile toxin.
SNARE cleavage is the action of tetanus and botulinum toxins.
ADP-ribosylation of EF-2 is the action of diphtheria toxin and Pseudomonas exotoxin A.

items.stem: A woman with trichomoniasis is treated with metronidazole. What else is required to prevent reinfection?
options: Treating her sexual partners as well
Douching after each course of treatment
items.rationale: Trichomoniasis is treated with metronidazole for the patient and partner(s), with testing for other STIs.
expl: Fluconazole does not treat or prevent trichomoniasis.
Douching does not prevent reinfection and can cause harm.
A test of cure within 48 hours is not required and would be too early.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A 2-year-old boy has had severe pyogenic infections since infancy and now has Pneumocystis pneumonia. Serum IgM is high, while IgG, IgA, and IgE are very low. What is the underlying cause?
options: Mutation of BTK in B-cell precursors
Mutation of the ATM DNA-repair gene
Defective CD40 ligand on helper T cells
items.rationale: Hyper-IgM syndrome is most commonly due to defective CD40L on helper T cells, an X-linked recessive class-switching defect; it causes severe pyogenic infections early in life and opportunistic infections with Pneumocystis, Cryptosporidium, and CMV, with normal or high IgM and very low IgG, IgA, and IgE.
expl: BTK mutation lowers all immunoglobulin classes, including IgM.
ATM mutation causes ataxia-telangiectasia with IgA deficiency.
NADPH oxidase defects do not change immunoglobulin levels.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: Sputum from a patient with Legionnaires disease shows many neutrophils but few organisms on Gram stain. What best explains the finding?
options: Legionella is mainly intracellular and stains poorly
Legionella is too thin to be resolved
Legionella lacks a cell wall entirely
items.rationale: Legionella, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Bartonella, Anaplasma, and Ehrlichia are primarily intracellular and stain poorly with Gram stain; Legionella is detected by urinary antigen or culture on special media.
expl: Acid-fastness explains poor Gram staining of mycobacteria.
Being too thin explains poor staining of Treponema and Leptospira.
Lack of a cell wall explains poor staining of Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma.
